name: Confounding
short: A hidden third factor drives both exposure and outcome.
text: A third factor causes both the exposure and the outcome, faking or hiding an effect.
example: Coffee drinkers seemed to get more lung cancer, because coffee drinkers smoked more.

ref.cite: Greenland et al. (1999). Confounding and Collapsibility in Causal Inference. Statistical Science.

name: Confounding by indication
short: The sickest get the treatment, so the treatment looks harmful.
text: The reason someone is treated is itself linked to the outcome, so treatment looks harmful (or helpful) when it isn't.
example: In routine records, a heart drug looked deadly because doctors reserved it for the sickest patients.

ref.cite: Kyriacou & Lewis (2016). Confounding by Indication in Clinical Research. JAMA.

name: Selection bias
short: Who ends up in the sample depends on what you're studying.
text: Who gets into (or stays in) the sample depends on the exposure, the outcome, or both.
example: Literary Digest (1936) mailed 10 million ballots, largely to phone and car owners; the 2.4 million returned predicted Landon. Roosevelt won in a landslide.

ref.cite: Hernán et al. (2004). A Structural Approach to Selection Bias. Epidemiology.

name: Attrition & missing data
short: The people who drop out are not like the people who stay.
text: Participants drop out, or data go missing, for reasons related to the treatment or the outcome.
example: In a weight-loss trial, the people who weren't losing weight quietly stopped coming. The remaining group looked great.

ref.cite: Sterne et al. (2009). Multiple imputation for missing data in epidemiological and clinical research: potential and pitfalls. BMJ.

name: Recall bias
short: Cases remember their past differently from controls.
text: People with the outcome remember or report past exposures differently from people without it.
example: Mothers of babies with birth defects search their memory harder for medicines taken in pregnancy.

ref.cite: Coughlin (1990). Recall bias in epidemiologic studies. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology.

name: Measurement error
short: The instrument is noisy, biased or drifting.
text: The instrument is noisy, biased, drifting, or used differently across groups or over time.
example: Self-reported diets underestimate energy intake, and more so in some groups than in others.

ref.cite: Hutcheon et al. (2010). Random measurement error and regression dilution bias. BMJ.

name: Reverse causation
short: The outcome is causing the 'cause'.
text: The outcome (or its early stages) causes the exposure, not the other way round.
example: Thin older adults die sooner, partly because illness causes weight loss years before death.

ref.cite: Hill (1965). The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?. Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine.

name: Regression to the mean
short: Extreme values drift back toward average on their own.
text: Units picked for extreme values drift back toward average on re-measurement, with or without any intervention.
example: Pupils chosen for tutoring after their worst-ever test score improve next time, tutoring or not.

ref.cite: Barnett (2004). Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it. International Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Expectation effects
short: Knowing who got what changes the result.
text: Placebo, Hawthorne and observer effects: knowing who got what changes behaviour, symptoms or readings.
example: Moseley et al. (2002): sham knee arthroscopy relieved pain as much as the real operation.

ref.cite: Hrobjartsson et al. (2012). Observer bias in randomised clinical trials with binary outcomes: systematic review of trials with both blinded and non-blinded outcome assessors. BMJ.

name: Contamination & spillover
short: The control group catches the intervention.
text: The control group gets exposed to the intervention, or effects spill over between units, diluting the difference.
example: Control-group teachers borrowed the new curriculum from their colleagues down the hall.

ref.cite: Torgerson (2001). Contamination in trials: is cluster randomisation the answer?. BMJ.

name: Immortal time bias
short: The treated get credit for time in which they couldn't have died.
text: The treated group is credited with follow-up time during which, by definition, the outcome couldn't happen.
example: Oscar winners seemed to live ~4 years longer than nominees, partly because you must survive long enough to win.

ref.cite: Suissa (2008). Immortal Time Bias in Pharmacoepidemiology. American Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Collider bias
short: Selecting on a common effect invents a link.
text: Selecting or adjusting on a common effect of exposure and outcome creates a spurious association (Berkson's bias).
example: Among hospital patients, two unrelated diseases look linked, because having either one gets you admitted.

ref.cite: Cole et al. (2009). Illustrating bias due to conditioning on a collider. International Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Ecological fallacy
short: What's true of groups needn't be true of their members.
text: Concluding something about individuals from an association seen only between groups.
example: Robinson (1950): US states with more immigrants had higher literacy, though immigrants themselves were less often literate.

ref.cite: Robinson (1950). Ecological Correlations and the Behavior of Individuals. American Sociological Review.

name: Unit-of-analysis error
short: Groups were randomized, but individuals were counted.
text: Groups are randomized or sampled, but individuals are analysed as if independent. False precision follows.
example: A trial randomizing 10 schools analysed 3,000 pupils as independent and reported impossibly narrow confidence intervals.

ref.cite: Bland & Kerry (1997). Trials randomised in clusters. BMJ.

name: Survivorship bias
short: You only see the ones that made it back.
text: Only the survivors, successes or still-present units are observed; the failures are invisible.
example: Wald, WWII: armour belongs where returning bombers had no bullet holes, because the planes hit there never came back.

ref.cite: Mangel & Samaniego (1984). Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability. Journal of the American Statistical Association.

name: Publication bias
short: The null results are still in the drawer.
text: Positive results get published, null results stay in the drawer, and the literature lies by omission.
example: Turner et al. (2008): almost all positive antidepressant trials were published; most negative ones were not, or were spun.

ref.cite: Rosenthal (1979). The file drawer problem and tolerance for null results. Psychological Bulletin.

name: Unvetted sources
short: Nobody checked it, and the author may be selling something.
text: Grey sources skip peer review: vendors, consultants and enthusiasts can publish striking claims with no visible method or data.
example: The Standish CHAOS reports' famous IT-project failure rates were cited for years; Eveleens & Verhoef (2010) showed their definitions skewed the figures.

ref.cite: Eveleens & Verhoef (2010). The rise and fall of the Chaos report figures. IEEE Software.

name: Forking paths & p-hacking
short: Try enough analyses and one of them will be 'significant'.
text: Flexible choices of outcomes, subgroups and analyses, or peeking at the data, until something is 'significant'.
example: Simmons et al. (2011) used flexible analyses to 'show' that listening to a Beatles song made people younger.

ref.cite: Simmons et al. (2011). False-Positive Psychology. Psychological Science.

name: Low power
short: Too small to see the effect, and too noisy to trust a hit.
text: Too few units to detect a realistic effect; the 'significant' findings that do emerge are exaggerated.
example: Button et al. (2013): median statistical power in neuroscience studies was about 21%.

ref.cite: Button et al. (2013). Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience. Nature Reviews Neuroscience.

name: Overfitting & leakage
short: The model memorized the test.
text: The model memorizes noise, or sees information from the test data or the future, and fails in the real world.
example: Chest X-ray AI learned to recognize which hospital (and scanner) an image came from, not the disease (Zech et al., 2018).

ref.cite: Kaufman et al. (2012). Leakage in data mining. ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data.

name: Spectrum bias
short: It was only tested on the obvious cases.
text: A test or rater is evaluated on clear-cut cases and obvious non-cases rather than on the realistic mix of patients or samples.
example: Tests that look near-perfect on severe cases vs. healthy volunteers falter on the mild, ambiguous patients in real clinics.

ref.cite: Ransohoff & Feinstein (1978). Problems of Spectrum and Bias in Evaluating the Efficacy of Diagnostic Tests. New England Journal of Medicine.

name: History & secular trends
short: Something else changed at the same time.
text: Something else changed at the same time (a trend, the season, another policy) and takes the credit or the blame.
example: A hospital's hygiene campaign coincided with a nationwide fall in infections and got credit for both.

ref.cite: Campbell (1957). Factors relevant to the validity of experiments in social settings. Psychological Bulletin.

name: Carryover
short: The first treatment lingers into the second period.
text: The effect of an earlier treatment period bleeds into the next one.
example: A drug's effect lingered into the placebo period of a crossover trial, making placebo look effective.

ref.cite: Wellek & Blettner (2012). On the Proper Use of the Crossover Design in Clinical Trials. Deutsches Ärzteblatt international.

name: Researcher bias
short: You see what you expected to see.
text: The analyst's expectations, attachments or position shape what is seen, coded and reported.
example: Analysts who knew the hypothesis read ambiguous interview passages as supporting it.

ref.cite: Mays & Pope (2000). Qualitative research in health care: Assessing quality in qualitative research. BMJ.

name: Limited generalizability
short: True here, but maybe not anywhere else.
text: The sample, setting or conditions differ from where the results will be used.
example: Henrich et al. (2010): most psychology findings came from WEIRD samples (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic).

ref.cite: Rothwell (2005). External validity of randomised controlled trials: “To whom do the results of this trial apply?”. The Lancet.

name: Apples & oranges
short: Pooling apples with oranges.
text: Studies, populations or interventions pooled together differ so much that the average means little.
example: Pooling trials of different drugs, doses and patients gives a precise average of nothing in particular.

ref.cite: Higgins & Thompson (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine.

name: Unvalidated model
short: The model rests on assumptions nobody checked.
text: A model, derivation or simulation rests on unchecked assumptions, wrong inputs or numerical artifacts.
example: The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999: one team's software used imperial units, the other expected metric.

ref.cite: Box (1976). Science and Statistics. Journal of the American Statistical Association.

name: Wrong construct
short: You measured a proxy, not the real thing.
text: You measure a proxy or surrogate that doesn't capture what you actually care about.
example: CAST (1989): drugs that suppressed irregular heartbeats on monitors increased deaths.

ref.cite: Messick (1995). Validity of psychological assessment: Validation of inferences from persons' responses and performances as scientific inquiry into score meaning. American Psychologist.

name: Thin data
short: Too few voices to support the story.
text: Too few or too similar cases and voices; conclusions are drawn before the data are rich enough.
example: Six interviews with enthusiastic early adopters produced a 'theory' that collapsed when sceptics were interviewed.

ref.cite: Saunders et al. (2017). Saturation in qualitative research: exploring its conceptualization and operationalization. Quality & Quantity.
